description: The format library: every short video is labelled on four separate axes (format = the story structure, editing = how it looks on screen, visualHook = what the first two seconds show, series = a repeatable episode). Entries here are the starter set that ships with the plugin; a brand's own taken-apart videos are added as examples under the same ids in its library (workspaces/<brand>/library/intelligence/posts.jsonl).

format.name: Tutorial
format.definition: Shows the viewer how to do one thing, step by step, so they can copy it.
format.whyItWorks: It promises a concrete result, so people watch to the last step and save it to use later.

format.name: Listicle or ranking
format.definition: A numbered list or a ranking: 5 tools, 3 mistakes, the best to the worst.
format.whyItWorks: The number tells the viewer what they will get and how long it lasts, and every item is a small payoff that keeps them watching.

format.name: Breakdown
format.definition: Takes apart something real (an ad, a result, a competitor's move, a product) and says why it works.
format.whyItWorks: It feeds curiosity about the how, and it shows that you know the subject without saying so.

format.name: Story time
format.definition: A story told from the start with a turn and a lesson, about a person, a customer or the brand.
format.whyItWorks: People stay to find out how it ends, and remember the lesson through the person.

format.name: Before and after
format.definition: Shows the problem state, then the result, and what changed in between.
format.whyItWorks: The gap is visible in seconds, and the viewer pictures themselves on the after side.

format.name: Myth vs fact
format.definition: States a common belief, then corrects it with the truth and the proof.
format.whyItWorks: A contradiction creates tension, and people share it because it settles an argument or makes them feel informed.

format.name: Comparison
format.definition: Puts two options side by side (this against that, the old way against the new way) and picks one.
format.whyItWorks: It helps a choice, and people who search for X against Y are close to deciding.

format.name: Case study
format.definition: One real customer or project: where they started, what was done, and the numbers.
format.whyItWorks: Specific numbers are believable, and a named result is the proof a doubtful buyer looks for.

format.name: POV
format.definition: Puts the viewer inside a first-person moment, acted out in a short scene ("POV: you ...").
format.whyItWorks: The viewer recognises their own situation at once and stops scrolling.

format.name: Reaction or green screen
format.definition: The presenter reacts to, or stands in front of, another video, post or news item and adds a clear take.
format.whyItWorks: It borrows the attention of something already popular and adds an opinion.

format.name: Day in the life
format.definition: Follows a person or the team through a day or a task and shows the work behind the brand.
format.whyItWorks: It builds trust and familiarity, and it is easy to make from real footage.

format.name: Q and A
format.definition: Answers one real question from a customer or a comment, directly.
format.whyItWorks: The question proves there is demand, and the answer speaks to everyone with the same doubt.

editing.name: Talking head with captions
editing.definition: A person speaks to camera, with burned-in captions and light cuts.
editing.whyItWorks: A voice and a face carry trust, and captions keep it watchable on mute.

editing.name: Faceless b-roll and voice-over
editing.definition: A voice-over (real or made) over product, screen or stock footage, with nobody on camera.
editing.whyItWorks: No presenter is needed, so it is quick to make in volume, and the footage keeps the picture changing.

editing.name: Screen recording
editing.definition: The screen is the video: a walk through a tool, page or workflow, usually with a voice-over.
editing.whyItWorks: It shows the real thing working, which suits software and how-to topics.

editing.name: Split screen
editing.definition: Two pictures at once: before and after, this and that, or a presenter over something playing.
editing.whyItWorks: It gives the eye a comparison or a second thing to hold on to.

editing.name: Text-led
editing.definition: Big on-screen text does the talking, over simple footage, a whiteboard or a plain background.
editing.whyItWorks: It works without sound and without a presenter, and the reading pace sets the rhythm.

editing.name: Cinematic
editing.definition: Planned shots, controlled light and sound design, with a polished look.
editing.whyItWorks: It signals quality and brand feel, and suits products and places.

editing.name: Lo-fi phone
editing.definition: Shot on a phone, handheld, in natural light, with little or no polish.
editing.whyItWorks: It feels like a friend's video, not an ad, which lowers the viewer's guard.

editing.name: Animated or motion graphics
editing.definition: Animated shapes, icons and diagrams explain an idea, with no live footage needed.
editing.whyItWorks: It makes an abstract idea visible and keeps one look across every post.

visualHook.name: Object in hand
visualHook.definition: The first frame shows a real object held up to the camera.
visualHook.whyItWorks: A physical thing is concrete and makes the viewer ask what it is and why it is being shown.

visualHook.name: Pattern interrupt
visualHook.definition: Something unexpected in the first second: a sudden move, an odd prop, a jump straight into the scene.
visualHook.whyItWorks: It breaks the scrolling rhythm and buys the next two seconds.

visualHook.name: Text-only shock line
visualHook.definition: A bold line of text on a plain frame, such as "Stop doing this."
visualHook.whyItWorks: It reads at a glance, needs no setup, and opens a question.

visualHook.name: Result first
visualHook.definition: Opens on the finished result or the number, then goes back to show how it happened.
visualHook.whyItWorks: The payoff comes upfront, so the viewer stays for the how.

visualHook.name: Subject motion
visualHook.definition: The first frame is something moving: pouring, walking towards the camera, a quick change.
visualHook.whyItWorks: Movement catches the eye in a feed of still frames.

visualHook.name: Face close-up
visualHook.definition: A tight shot of a face with direct eye contact and an expression.
visualHook.whyItWorks: Faces are read instantly, and a direct look feels personal.

visualHook.name: Prop or demo
visualHook.definition: The first seconds show the product or a prop actually being used.
visualHook.whyItWorks: There is proof from the first frame of what it is and what it does.

visualHook.name: Before and after flash
visualHook.definition: A quick cut between the before and the after in the opening second.
visualHook.whyItWorks: The contrast lands before the voice does.

series.name: Case study series
series.definition: One customer or project per post, always told in the same order.
series.whyItWorks: Viewers know what to expect and come back, and every episode is proof.

series.name: Myth of the week
series.definition: One myth of the field busted per week, in the same format.
series.whyItWorks: A weekly habit trains the audience to return, and each myth is easy to find new material for.

series.name: Tool of the day
series.definition: One tool, product or tip per post, always in the same quick shape.
series.whyItWorks: It is easy to repeat, and each episode stands alone for a new viewer.

series.name: Teardown series
series.definition: One example (an ad, a page, a post) taken apart per episode.
series.whyItWorks: The repeated structure builds authority, and there is always a new example to take apart.

legacyNote: legacyFormats maps the container ids of pipeline/playbooks/visual-formats.md (still used by the stage pairing table and post.md format_id) onto the axes above, so an older concept or filed job still lands on the right rows.
